lead: Every part of an aircraft exists to carry a load from where it is applied to where it can be reacted. Wing skin collects air pressure, hands it to stringers, stringers hand it to ribs, ribs hand it to spars, spars hand it to the wing root fittings, the fittings hand it to the fuselage, and the fuselage balances it at its frames and bulkheads. Read the airframe this way — as a chain of load paths — and the long list of member names becomes a short list of jobs. Stress engineers, designers and maintenance crews all work from this map.
prereq: You need: force, pressure and equilibrium from school physics, nothing more.

sections.h3: The five groups and what each is for

blocks.text: The airframe is everything in the aircraft that carries load: skin, skeleton and joints. It does not include engine internals, avionics or fuel plumbing. It is easier to learn as five groups.

The wing makes lift and passes it inboard to the fuselage. The fuselage carries the payload — passengers and cargo — takes the reactions from wing and tail, and holds the cabin pressure. The empennage, or tail unit, has the fin, which makes side force, and the tailplane, which makes pitch balance. The landing gear takes ground reaction, braking and side loads. Engine mounts and nacelles take thrust and engine weight.

A load path is the route a force takes through the structure. Every member collects a load from a thinner, more flexible neighbour and hands it to a stiffer, stronger one, until the force is balanced at a joint, a bulkhead or the wing root. Nothing in an airframe carries load for its own sake.
Inside the groups sit the named members. Some syllabi call the skin the covering, or the stressed skin.

items: Skin: the outer surface. Keeps the aerodynamic shape and, in semi-monocoque construction, carries pressure, shear and part of the bending.
Stringers: light stiffeners riveted to the inside of the skin, running spanwise in a wing and lengthwise in a fuselage. They support the skin between ribs or frames and take axial load with it.
Longerons: heavy longitudinal fuselage members. With the skin they carry fuselage bending.
Ribs: chordwise wing members. They hold the aerofoil shape, support the stringers and pass load to the spars.
Frames: rings inside the fuselage. They keep the cross-section shape, support the skin and take floor and cabin loads.
Bulkheads: solid partitions. A pressure bulkhead closes the cabin at the nose and the aft end and takes the whole cabin pressure.
Spars: the main spanwise wing beams. The caps (top and bottom flanges) take bending; the thin web takes shear.
Doublers: extra plates around a cut-out, door or joint. They spread load around the opening so the thin skin is not overstressed.
Fittings: compact machined or forged parts that join one member to another — wing root to fuselage, spar to rib, gear to wing.
Floor beams: transverse beams that carry the cabin floor and its loads to the frames.

sections.h3: Skin to stringer to rib to spar to fuselage

items: Air pressure acts normally on a skin panel of area A. The skin bends between its supports and carries the pressure as a distributed load.
The skin passes the load to the stringers, which run spanwise beneath it.
The stringers pass it to the ribs, which run chordwise across the wing.
The ribs pass it to the front and rear spars.
The spar caps take it as bending — compression in the top cap, tension in the bottom cap — and the spar web takes it as shear, all the way to the root.
Root fittings pass it into fuselage frames and bulkheads.
The fuselage carries it as a beam: skin and longerons in bending, frames holding the cross-section and stopping the skin from buckling, floor beams feeding cabin loads into the frames.

blocks.text: P = p × A        P<sub>s</sub> = P / n
blocks.where: p is the normal pressure on the panel in N/m² (Pa); A is the panel area in m²; P is the total load on the panel in N; n is the number of stringers sharing it; P<sub>s</sub> is the load per stringer in N.

blocks.text: Doublers and fittings belong to the chain too. A doubler around a door or an antenna cut-out spreads the same force over more skin, so the thin panel is not overstressed. Every rivet row, bonded lap and bolted fitting must pass that force with a margin, which is why fabrication of structural components decides real strength. The wing as a complete torsion box is worked out in typical wing and fuselage structures.

Below, the load path chain from air pressure to the fuselage frame.

examples.question: A wing skin panel is 0.6 m long spanwise and 0.4 m wide chordwise. The normal air pressure on it is 15 kPa. Four spanwise stringers share the panel load equally. Find the total load on the panel and the load carried by each stringer.
steps: Pressure p = 15 kPa = 15 000 N/m², because 1 Pa = 1 N/m².
Panel load P = p × A = 15 000 × 0.24 = 3 600 N.
Load per stringer P<sub>s</sub> = P / n = 3 600 / 4 = 900 N.
Check: 4 × 900 = 3 600 N, which matches the panel load.
examples.answer: The panel carries 3 600 N in total, and each of the four stringers carries 900 N.
examples.check:
area = 0.6 * 0.4
p = 15000.0
P = p * area
n = 4
per_stringer = P / n
print(round(area, 4))
print(round(P, 4))
print(round(per_stringer, 4))

examples.question: The front spar of a wing carries, at its root, a bending moment M = 288 kN·m and a shear force V = 72 kN (the root values found in Shear force and bending moment distribution on wings). The centroids of its top and bottom caps are h = 0.40 m apart and the web is 3 mm thick. Assume the caps carry all the bending and the web carries all the shear. Find the axial force in each cap, the cap area needed at an allowable stress of 400 MPa, and the average shear stress in the web.
steps: The caps act as a couple: a compressive force F in the top cap and an equal tensile force F in the bottom cap, h apart. Their moment F × h must equal M.
Cap force F = M / h = 288 000 N·m ÷ 0.40 m = 720 000 N = 720 kN (compression in the top cap, tension in the bottom cap).
Check: F × h = 720 kN × 0.40 m = 288 kN·m, the moment we started with.
examples.answer: Each cap carries 720 kN (top in compression, bottom in tension) and needs about 1800 mm² at 400 MPa; the web carries an average shear stress of 60 MPa.

traps: Ribs and spars swapped. Ribs run chordwise and keep the aerofoil shape, passing load to the spars; spars run spanwise and take the bending.
Treating the skin as shape only. In semi-monocoque construction the skin is a primary load path and carries pressure, shear and part of the bending.
Frames and longerons swapped. Frames are rings that hold the cross-section; longerons are longitudinal members that take bending.
Calling every ring a bulkhead. A bulkhead is a solid partition, and a pressure bulkhead carries the whole cabin pressure.
Using the full spar depth or the skin-to-skin depth in F = M/h. Use the distance between the cap centroids; a larger h gives a cap force that is too small.
Pressure unit slip. 15 kPa is 15 000 Pa, not 15 Pa; a wrong conversion makes the answer 1000 times too small.

quiz.q: Name the five main groups of an airframe and give one job of each.
quiz.a: Wing makes lift and carries it inboard; fuselage carries payload and reacts wing and tail loads; empennage gives stability and control; landing gear takes ground loads; engine mounts take thrust and engine weight.

quiz.q: What is a longeron, and how does it differ from a frame?
quiz.a: A longeron is a longitudinal fuselage member that takes bending with the skin. A frame is a transverse ring that keeps the cross-section and supports the skin.

quiz.q: Why does a wing load pass through several members instead of going straight from skin to fuselage?
quiz.a: Each member is thin and can carry only a limited load over a limited length. Stiffeners, ribs and spars collect and concentrate the load step by step until a few strong root fittings can take it. Doing it in one jump would need a very heavy skin.

quiz.q: Why are spar caps placed at the top and bottom of a spar instead of at mid-height?
quiz.a: Bending gives compression on one face and tension on the other, largest at the outer fibres. Material far from the neutral axis gives the most bending stiffness and strength for the least weight; the thin web between the caps carries shear.

quiz.q: A spar root carries M = 150 kN·m. Its cap centroids are 0.30 m apart and the allowable cap stress is 375 MPa. Find the cap force and the cap area.
A 200 mm hole is cut in a pressurized fuselage skin for an antenna. Using load paths, explain the doubler fitted around it and what fails without one.
quiz.a: The hole removes skin area, so the same hoop and longitudinal tension must pass through a narrower path; local stress rises and cracks start at the cut edge. The doubler adds material around the opening, spreads the force back into the full panel and its rivet rows must be sized for the diverted load. Without it, the panel would be overstressed and fatigue life would drop.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry builds this same load-path map as a finite element model, and member sizes come out of it. Strain gauges on in-service aircraft show how the real paths share force, which feeds damage-tolerance checks. Topology optimization and additive manufacturing now give brackets a shape that follows the load path rather than a machinist's convenience. Composite wings cure skin and stiffeners into one part, so many of the joints that once defined the path disappear. Search terms: structural idealization, load path, damage tolerance, topology optimization.
